repos.title: Mathematical Supplement for the $\texttt{gsplat}$ Library
repos.paper_summary: The gsplat library provides a modular Python implementation of differentiable Gaussian splatting, releasing the complete mathematical derivations for its forward and backward passes. The method renders 3D Gaussians by projecting their means and covariances into pixel space using a first-order Taylor expansion, then composites them front-to-back via alpha blending. The paper derives the analytical gradients for all Gaussian parameters—including position, scale, rotation, opacity, and color—using matrix calculus and the Frobenius inner product to facilitate efficient backpropagation. This allows users to modify specific components of the computational graph within the `nerfstudio` framework. Because the projection relies on a linear approximation of the perspective transform, the resulting 2D covariance is an approximation rather than an exact projection. The report serves as a reference for the existing algorithm introduced by Kerbl et al. (2023) and does not present new empirical benchmarks or quantitative performance comparisons against other rendering methods.

repos.title: LLM4Decompile: Decompiling Binary Code with Large Language Models
repos.paper_summary:
LLM4Decompile is a series of open-source large language models, ranging from 1.3B to 33B parameters, trained to decompile x86 binary code into C source code. The authors initialize the models with DeepSeek-Coder checkpoints and fine-tune them using two distinct strategies: End2end-Decompile, which maps disassembled assembly directly to source code, and Refined-Decompile, which refines pseudo-code generated by Ghidra. Training data consists of approximately 7 billion tokens of compilable functions and 572 million tokens of executable functions derived from ExeBench, augmented across compiler optimization levels O0 through O3.

On the HumanEval-Decompile benchmark, LLM4Decompile-End-6.7B achieves a 45.4% re-executability rate, compared to 16.0% for GPT-4o and 20.1% for Ghidra. On ExeBench, it reaches 18.0%, while GPT-4o reaches 3.8%. The LLM4Decompile-Ref-6.7B model improves upon Ghidra’s output by 16.2% over the direct end-to-end approach. Under control flow flattening obfuscation, the success rate drops to 5.2%. The study is limited to C code on the x86 platform, and the 33B model was only partially trained due to resource constraints.

repos.title: An Open and Comprehensive Pipeline for Unified Object Grounding and Detection
repos.paper_summary: MM-Grounding-DINO is an open-source pipeline for unified object grounding and detection, built on the MMDetection toolbox. It reproduces the Grounding-DINO architecture, which uses a Swin Transformer image backbone and BERT text encoder with a cross-modality decoder, while replacing the proprietary Cap4M pre-training dataset with GRIT and V3Det. The model is trained on 15 datasets covering Open-Vocabulary Detection, Phrase Grounding, and Referring Expression Comprehension. In zero-shot evaluation, MM-Grounding-DINO-Tiny achieves 50.6 mAP on COCO and 41.4 AP on LVIS mini, outperforming the original Grounding-DINO-Tiny by 2.2 and 12.6 points respectively. Fine-tuning on COCO yields 58.2 mAP after 12 epochs. A limitation is that the GRIT dataset contains noisy annotations, including abstract phrases and full-image bounding boxes, which provides limited benefit for standard detection tasks compared to V3Det.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Grounding-DINO's training code is unreleased, so the authors rebuild it in MMDetection and extend benchmarks for three grounding tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Approach
digest_headlines.headline: Grounding-DINO's cross-modality architecture is kept, with a bias added to the contrastive embedding and random negative samples in augmentation.

digest_headlines.heading: Main Results
digest_headlines.headline: Zero-shot tests show the Tiny variants beat Grounding-DINO-Tiny on detection and referring-expression benchmarks, with the largest gains on the long-tail benchmark.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude the open pipeline matches or beats the Grounding-DINO baseline and release it as a shared resource.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix adds threshold sweeps, per-dataset tables for three benchmarks, open-vocabulary fine-tuning results and failure-case visualizations.

repos.title: Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision
repos.paper_summary:
Whisper is a family of encoder-decoder Transformer models trained on 680,000 hours of weakly supervised multilingual and multitask audio data. The system performs speech recognition, translation, language identification, and voice activity detection by conditioning the decoder on task-specific tokens. The paper reports that zero-shot Whisper Large V2 achieves an average word error rate (WER) of 12.8% across 13 English datasets, representing a 55.2% relative error reduction compared to wav2vec 2.0 Large. On LibriSpeech test-clean, both models achieve a WER of 2.7%, but Whisper generalizes significantly better to out-of-distribution data such as CHiME-6 (25.5% WER vs 65.8%). For X-to-English translation, Whisper achieves 29.1 BLEU on CoVoST2 without using any training data from that benchmark.

The dataset includes 117,000 hours for 96 languages and 125,000 hours of translation pairs. Performance scales with model size and dataset volume, though English recognition shows diminishing returns near human-level accuracy. Limitations include poor performance on low-resource languages due to insufficient training data per language, and remaining decoding errors in long-form transcription such as repetition loops and hallucinations.

repos.title: Chronos: Learning the Language of Time Series
repos.paper_summary:
Chronos is a pretrained probabilistic time series forecasting framework that adapts standard transformer language models to univariate forecasting. The method converts real-valued time series into discrete tokens by mean-scaling and quantizing values into 4,096 uniform bins. These token sequences are fed into T5 or GPT-2 architectures, which are trained via cross-entropy loss without architectural modifications. The authors pretrain models ranging from 20M to 710M parameters on 28 public datasets augmented with TSMixup convex combinations and KernelSynth Gaussian process synthetic data.

On a benchmark of 42 datasets, Chronos outperforms local statistical models like AutoARIMA and task-specific deep learning baselines such as PatchTST in both in-domain and zero-shot settings. On 27 unseen zero-shot datasets, the 710M parameter model achieves aggregated relative WQL scores comparable to methods specifically trained on those tasks. A limitation is that the fixed vocabulary restricts predictions to the training value range, potentially impairing performance on strongly trending series. Additionally, larger models exhibit slower inference times than lightweight local forecasters.

repos.title: The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction
repos.paper_summary: Edge0 is a streaming inference engine for 35B-class mixture-of-experts models on a 24 GB consumer machine. Expert weights stay on SSD and are memory-mapped on demand, so peak memory tracks the active experts, not all parameters. A per-layer prerouter head predicts the next layer's routing one token ahead, so expert reads overlap the current forward pass. The prediction is used as the routing itself, so the staged experts match the routed experts and none are dropped. An unmerged int4 recovery LoRA, distilled from the fp16 teacher on the student routing path, recovers quality lost to quantization and routing replacement. On a Mac mini M4 Pro with 24 GB, the 35B tier decodes at 20.4 tok/s with 2.9 GiB peak active memory, and the 8B tier at 28.0 tok/s with 1.5 GiB. On OpenCompass, the 35B tier averages 79.2 against 83.2 for its fp16 base, and the 8B tier 69.9 against 72.7. Limitations: AIME loses 6.1 points (35B) and 10.0 points (8B), requests are served one at a time, and CPU graph building sets a 44 ms per-step floor.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Storing 35B-class MoE weights on a 24 GB machine is the bottleneck, so Edge0 keeps experts on SSD and streams them.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior offloading moves the weight footprint rather than shrinking it, and pre-gating schedules next-block experts too late for a streaming engine.

digest_headlines.heading: System Design
digest_headlines.headline: A 40-layer MoE needs 16.9 GiB of routed experts, so Edge0 mmaps them from SSD across four executor paths.

digest_headlines.heading: Training
digest_headlines.headline: Three training phases make the model work under replaced routing: head distillation, fine-tuning on the student path, and on-policy distillation.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Both tiers average within a few points of fp16 bases, and the prerouter adds +80 to +84% decode where weights do not fit.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Decode has a 44 ms per-step floor from graph building, quality loss concentrates in long-chain reasoning, and one backend exists.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: A 35B MoE runs at 20 tok/s in 3 GiB on a 24 GB desktop, with framework, checkpoints, and adapters open source.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives the softmax-top-k and sigmoid-group routing formulas and the incremental-stack assembly A/B results.

repos.title: Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows
repos.paper_summary:
Swin Transformer is a hierarchical vision Transformer backbone that computes self-attention within non-overlapping local windows, shifting the window partition by $(\lfloor M/2 \rfloor, \lfloor M/2 \rfloor)$ between consecutive layers to enable cross-window connections while maintaining linear computational complexity with respect to image size. The architecture splits images into $4 \times 4$ patches and progressively merges them across four stages to produce feature maps at resolutions of $H/4$, $H/8$, $H/16$, and $H/32$. A relative position bias is added to the attention scores, parameterized by a matrix of size $(2M-1) \times (2M-1)$.

On ImageNet-1K, Swin-L achieves 87.3% top-1 accuracy after pre-training on ImageNet-22K. For object detection on COCO test-dev, it reaches 58.7 box AP and 51.1 mask AP, surpassing previous best results by +2.7 box AP and +2.6 mask AP. On ADE20K semantic segmentation, it obtains 53.5 mIoU, an improvement of +3.2 mIoU over the prior best model. Ablations show that shifted windows contribute +1.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K and +2.8 mIoU on ADE20K compared to static windows. The cyclic-shift implementation for efficient batch computation provides a 13–18% speed-up over naive padding.

repos.title: OpenPose: Realtime Multi-Person 2D Pose Estimation using Part Affinity Fields
repos.paper_summary:
OpenPose is a bottom-up system for realtime multi-person 2D pose estimation that uses Part Affinity Fields (PAFs) to associate body parts with individuals. The method employs a multi-stage CNN, initialized from VGG-19, to predict confidence maps for part locations and PAFs, which are 2D vector fields encoding limb position and orientation. A key architectural change refines only the PAFs across stages before predicting confidence maps, rather than refining both simultaneously; this reduces computation per stage by half while increasing accuracy by approximately 7% and runtime performance by 200%.

On the MPII dataset, the method achieves 75.6% mean Average Precision using a three-scale search, outperforming DeeperCut by 13% absolute mAP on the full test set. Inference takes 0.005 s per image on a subset of 288 images, compared to 230 s for DeeperCut. The authors also release a foot keypoint dataset containing 15K instances and show that a combined body-and-foot model maintains individual component accuracy while reducing inference time relative to sequential processing. Limitations include the reliance on greedy bipartite matching for parsing, which approximates the NP-hard global optimization problem, and the top-down approach used for hand and face detection based on body keypoints.

repos.title: Scientific Agent Skills: A Library of Procedural Knowledge for Research Agents
repos.paper_summary: Scientific Agent Skills is an open library of 163 procedural skills for research agents, spanning 16 areas including genomics, cheminformatics, medical imaging, study design and scientific communication. Each skill is a directory built around a versioned Markdown instruction file, often with reference documents and scripts. An agent loads the file only when a task calls for it. The paper is a resource description. It reports no task-level evaluation and no host selection rate. It measures two corpus properties at tag v2.65.0. The always-resident descriptions of all skills cost 7.1% of a 200,000-token window. The median of the 46 documented workflows fits within 23.9% of that window, although 29 of the 46 would overflow if every reference file were loaded. Lexical analysis finds a median nearest-neighbour cosine similarity of 0.15 between descriptions, with the closest pair at 0.40. Limitations include no evidence that skills improve agent outcomes, no measured selection accuracy, and uneven review, since 32 of 163 skills do not list the maintainers as author.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Agents often return working code that is not defensible, so the paper proposes a library of field-specific procedures packaged as agent skills.

digest_headlines.heading: What an agent skill is
digest_headlines.headline: Each skill is a directory whose instruction file is read only when relevant, keeping most documentation out of standing context.

digest_headlines.heading: What the library covers
digest_headlines.headline: The library's 163 skills cover 16 self-assigned categories, most shipping reference documents, and the workflows combine them unevenly.

digest_headlines.heading: Can descriptions distinguish among skills?
digest_headlines.headline: Most skill descriptions are lexically well separated, but a few neighbouring pairs remain close and some lack authored guidance.

digest_headlines.heading: Do the skills a workflow needs fit in context?
digest_headlines.headline: Documented workflows fit a 200,000-token window in their instruction files, but 29 of 46 overflow if every reference file loads.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: The paper reports no task-level evaluation, measures selection only as a lexical proxy, and does not test host portability.

digest_headlines.heading: Availability and citation
digest_headlines.headline: Work using the library should cite the paper and tag v2.65.0, and name each skill's metadata version.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendices list the tokenizer and token ledger, skill contents, category counts, routing sensitivity and installed-base estimate.
